query: Consider the following context: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) exhibit excellent properties such as high strength, good ductility, superior corrosion resistance, and thermal stability, making them highly promising for applications in the aerospace, energy, and automotive industries. Among them, the FeNiCrMn HEA demonstrates outstanding corrosion resistance while eliminating the expensive Co element present in the “Cantor” alloy, significantly reducing costs. However, current research on the FeNiCrMn HEA has primarily focused on its corrosion resistance, with relatively limited studies on its mechanical properties. In that context, which method can be used for the stated problem, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Processing FeNiCrMn HEA via additive manufacturing, specifically selective laser melting (SLM), will refine its microstructure and improve its mechanical properties (e.g., yield strength and ductility) compared to the conventional as-cast alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: FeNiCrMn high-entropy alloy produced by conventional melting/casting methods with a relatively coarse and heterogeneous grain structure.
generation.intervention: Re-fabrication of the FeNiCrMn HEA using selective laser melting (SLM) under controlled laser energy density and inert atmosphere conditions.
generation.conditions: Tests conducted at room temperature with similar sample geometries; SLM process parameters optimized to achieve uniform melting and rapid solidification.
generation.structural_mediator: A refined, homogeneous microstructure with finer grains and reduced segregation.
generation.mechanism: The rapid solidification in SLM is expected to promote grain refinement, enhance dislocation blocking, and increase solid-solution and grain boundary strengthening, leading to improved mechanical performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to conventionally cast samples, SLM-processed FeNiCrMn HEA will exhibit a statistically significant increase in yield strength and improved ductility.
generation.baseline: Mechanical properties (e.g., yield strength and ductility) of the conventionally cast FeNiCrMn HEA.
generation.boundary: The effect size may be limited by potential SLM-induced defects (e.g., porosity) or local inhomogeneities, and the optimum SLM processing window must be carefully maintained.
generation.uncertainty: While the evidence from similar HEA systems processed by additive manufacturing suggests this approach can improve mechanical properties, the exact quantitative improvement and the sensitivity to SLM parameters in the specific FeNiCrMn alloy remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrMn HEA samples: one set by conventional casting and another set by SLM with optimized parameters. Perform identical mechanical tests (tensile and compression tests) on both sets under controlled conditions. Additionally, carry out microstructural analysis using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) to quantify grain size and homogeneity.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the SLM-processed samples do not demonstrate a statistically significant improvement (e.g., >10% increase) in yield strength and a noticeably refined microstructure compared to the cast samples, then the hypothesis is refuted.

cited_evidence.text: Refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) have excellent mechanical properties, which could make them the substitutes of some superalloys. However, the high melting point of refractory HEAs leads to processing problems when using traditional processing techniques. In this study, a single BCC solid solution of NbMoTaW alloy was formed by selective laser melting (SLM) with a linear energy density of up to 2.83 J/mm. The composition distribution was analyzed, and the element with a lower melting point and lower density showed a negative deviation (no more than 5%) of the molar ratio in the formed alloy. The HEA shows an excellent microstructure, microhardness, and corrosion resistance performance compared with traditional superalloys, making it a new substitute metal with great application prospects in aerospace and energy fields.

Abstract The growing interest in refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) in the last decade is mainly due to their thermal stability, outstanding mechanical properties, and excellent corrosion resistance. However, currently HEAs are still not considered for use as common structural materials due to their inherent drawbacks in terms of processing and machining operations. The recent progress witnessed in additive manufacturing (AM) technologies has raised the option of producing complex components made of HEAs with minimal machining processes. So far, this could be achieved by using pre-alloyed powders of HEAs that were mainly produced by a conventional arc melting furnace (AMF) in the form of small compounds that were transformed into powder via a gas atomization process. To significantly reduce the production cost, the present study aims to analyze the ability to synthesize HEA WTaMoNbV via a laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) process using mixed elemental alloying powder as the raw material.
